classification_signals: Abstract: 'I propose a criticism... I suggest that nature should be treated... This thesis thus explores the capabilities... to reinterpret... in the form of a dichotomic reciprocity.' (p. 6)
Table of Contents: 'CHAPTER 4. REFRAMING ECOLOGICAL ETHICS IN ARCHITECTURE', 'CHAPTER 6. DESIGN COMPONENT' (p. 3)
Section: 'Lastly, and in addition to literature review and case study research this thesis takes an approach into reconceptualizing biomimesis in a design strategy.' (p. 11)
title: Dichotomic reciprocity: The practice of a more intimate biomimicry in architectural design

findings.antecedent: Human superiority and domination of the environment (Western cultural belief)
findings.consequent: Anthropogenic epoch, exploitation of natural resources and living beings
findings.quote: The superiority of man and his domination of the environment has ushered in a new geological and anthropogenic epoch, an unprecedented period in planetary history, where the exploitation of natural resources and living beings is the norm.

findings.antecedent: Dichotomic reciprocity (relationship between nature and designer, capacity for intervention)
findings.consequent: Framework of affective appreciation in culture
findings.quote: the capacity for intervention within this relationship to employ a framework of affective appreciation into the culture of today.

findings.antecedent: Western Judeo-Christian tradition (belief in human distinction and superiority)
findings.consequent: Human claim of dominance over nature
findings.quote: An interpretation of our hegemonistic act may arise from a belief in human distinction in the Western culture of Judeo-Christian tradition (Williams, 2010)... thus giving humans the “authority” to claim dominance over nature (Hendy, Glosik and Okech, 2005).

findings.quote: Continuous industrialization changed a scenario of cohabitation.

findings.antecedent: Human dominance, continuous urban growth, modernization, technological advancements
findings.consequent: Nature's vulnerability, 'invisible' barrier between man and nature
findings.quote: Humanity's action of dominance has forced nature to an ever more vulnerable position and... this encroachment has created an “invisible” barrier between man and nature.

findings.consequent: Largest contributor to negative effects on ecosystem services
findings.quote: the built environment after the industrial revolution was designed only for humans... and were made into an "operational apparatus for living” that would simultaneously become the largest contributor for negative effects on the ecosystem services.

findings.consequent: Favoring humans over conviviality and co-existence with nature
findings.quote: The understanding of ecological architecture and the movement of ‘green buildings' are very much still in favor of humans as opposed to conviviality and co-existence.

findings.antecedent: Nature's ingenuity (as understood by this thesis)
findings.consequent: Improved re-connectivity with nature, amelioration of 'abusive' culture, affective framework of relationship with nature
findings.quote: this thesis looks into expanding the understanding to include nature's ingenuity to improve re-connectivity with nature and to ameliorate the existing "abusive” culture into one that factors into it an affective framework of relationship with nature.

findings.antecedent: Biomimicry (borrowing life's blueprint, chemical recipes, ecosystem strategies)
findings.consequent: Sustainable solutions, integration of human species into natural processes of Earth
findings.quote: At its most transformative, biomimicry connects us in ways that integrate human species into the natural processes of Earth” (Baumesiter, Tocke, Dwyer, Ritters, Benyus, 2013).

minimum_safe_summary: This Master's thesis, 'Dichotomic reciprocity: The practice of a more intimate biomimicry in architectural design,' proposes a reinterpretation of biomimicry to foster an 'affective appreciation' and 'dichotomic reciprocity' between humans and nature, moving beyond an exploitative, efficiency-focused approach. It argues that Western cultures' historical dominance over nature has led to environmental degradation and an 'invisible barrier' between humans and the natural world. The thesis suggests that events like the COVID-19 pandemic have highlighted the need for a paradigm shift towards a more intimate co-existence, drawing on concepts like salutogenesis and the Oneness hypothesis to advocate for architectural design that promotes ecological synergy and human well-being intertwined with nature's flourishing. It includes a literature review, case study, and design component to explore these ideas.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper describes a conceptual causal chain where Western cultural beliefs in human superiority and environmental domination lead to the exploitation of natural resources and living beings, ultimately resulting in the Anthropogenic epoch.
